turns.user: got a panel interview thursday for a project coordinator job at a freight company. im a working parent so i can only prep after the kids are in bed, like 9-10pm. quick one: how long should each answer be? mine keep running like 5 minutes and i think i lose them
turns.assistant: Aim for roughly 60 to 90 seconds per answer, and two minutes is about the ceiling for a big behavioral question. Panels usually have three to five people and a set list of questions, so a five-minute answer eats the time for everyone else's questions and they start tuning out. A quick check: time yourself reading the answer out loud. If you're past two minutes, cut the background and the 'why this happened' part and get to what you did and what changed. Keep the result specific, something like 'the shipment was three days late, I rerouted two pallets, and the client didn't lose the order.'

turns.user: ok that helps. so what's the STAR thing everyone keeps saying
turns.assistant: STAR is a structure for behavioral answers. Situation is one or two sentences of context. Task is what you were responsible for. Action is what you specifically did, and it's the biggest part. Result is what happened, with a number if you have one. Most people spend too long on Situation and too little on Action, which is what interviewers are scoring. For a project coordinator role, your Actions might cover scheduling, chasing vendors, or clearing blockers. Write one story per STAR, then practice telling each in about 90 seconds.

turns.user: that didn't work for me last time tbh, i kept forgetting the result part
turns.assistant: That's really common, and it usually means the result got tacked on at the end when you were already tired. Try writing the result first. Finish the sentence 'because of what I did, ___ happened.' If you can't fill that blank with something concrete, the story probably needs a different example. A rough number is fine too: 'cut onboarding from two weeks to one' works. Then practice telling the story backwards from the result so you always land on it.

turns.user: ok wait what if i don't have a good result. like the project just kinda ended
turns.assistant: Then say what changed afterward and be honest about the outcome. 'The project was shelved after two quarters, but the vendor checklist I built was still in use a year later' is a real result. Interviewers mostly want to see how you think about outcomes. Don't invent a metric you can't defend, because the follow-up questions will find it. If the outcome is truly empty, pick a different story. Have at least three ready for different themes: conflict, deadline pressure, and a mistake you made.

turns.user: and if i only have like 3 evenings before thursday, what do i actually do
turns.assistant: Evening one: write four or five stories in STAR form as bullet points, and don't polish them. Evening two: say each one out loud, timed, and cut anything past two minutes. Evening three: do a full mock with a friend, or record yourself on your phone and watch it once. Also skim the company's recent news and the job posting, and pick two questions to ask them at the end. Forty-five focused minutes a night will get you further than rereading notes for hours.

turns.user: perfect. one more thing, what if they ask why i left my last job, which was because my old boss was awful. how do i say that without sounding bitter
turns.assistant: Keep it to one sentence about the reason, then pivot to what you're looking for. Something like: 'I was ready for more ownership, and my last role had limited room for that. I'm looking for a place where coordinators run projects end to end.' Don't name the boss or describe what happened, even if it was bad, because interviewers hear that as a red flag about you. If they press, say you'd rather focus on the role ahead, then give a positive example of what you want next.

turns.user: my sister is getting married in november and i'm supposed to give the maid of honor speech. im a working parent with two kids so i have basically no time. why do people say the speech should be short? like what's the actual reason, not just 'keep it brief'
turns.assistant: The main reason is attention. Wedding guests have been through the ceremony, cocktails and dinner, often after a long day of travel, and the room's patience drops off sharply after about three minutes. A short speech also makes the good moments land harder. A sharp story and a clear closing line hit better than a long run of memories. There's a practical side too: long speeches drift into inside jokes that only you and the bride understand, and the rest of the room checks out. Most good maid of honor speeches run four to five minutes, roughly 500 to 650 words spoken at a relaxed pace.

turns.user: that makes sense. wait so is the 5 min thing a hard rule or can i go longer if the story is good
turns.assistant: It's not a hard rule. If the story is strong, a bit longer is fine, but most rooms start to fidget somewhere around six or seven minutes. Length matters less than whether each part earns its place. If you're unsure, read it aloud once with a timer. If you're over six minutes, look for a story that repeats a point you already made and cut it. Also speak slower than feels natural, because nerves make people talk faster, and that alone can add a minute.

turns.user: can my landlord raise rent during a fixed 12 month lease in toronto or do they have to wait til it ends
turns.assistant: In Ontario, a landlord generally can't raise rent during a fixed-term lease unless the lease itself has a clause allowing it, and those clauses are uncommon. Once the lease rolls over into a period-to-period tenancy, the landlord can increase rent once every 12 months, with at least 90 days written notice. The amount is capped by the provincial rent increase guideline for most units, but that cap doesn't apply to every building, so check which rules cover your unit.

turns.user: ok what about units built after 2018, is it different
turns.assistant: Yes. For units first occupied after November 15, 2018, rent control under the Residential Tenancies Act doesn't apply, so the landlord can set the increase amount. The 12-month rule and the 90-day written notice still apply. Ask the landlord whether the unit is exempt, and you can check the rules on the Landlord and Tenant Board website if you want to confirm.

turns.user: lol ok my place is 2020 so no rent control. what if the new rent is like 15% more, can i just say no
turns.assistant: You can refuse an increase that isn't legally permitted, such as one with the wrong notice or one during a fixed term. For an exempt unit, a valid increase still applies even if it's large. If you just refuse to pay a valid increase, the landlord can file an L1 application with the Landlord and Tenant Board for non-payment, and that can end in an eviction order. Your realistic options are to negotiate, to offer a longer lease in exchange for a smaller increase, or to give notice and move.

turns.user: ok fine. if i negotiate what do i actually say, is there a script
turns.assistant: Something like this works: 'Hi [name], thanks for the notice on the increase. I'd like to stay long term. Would you consider [X]% if I sign a two-year lease?' Keep it calm and short, and bring a couple of comparable listings in your area with their rents. If they agree, get the new terms in writing, either as an amendment to your lease or a signed letter, so the number is enforceable.

turns.user: we're going to japan in april for 10 days, flying into tokyo. quick q: how many days should we give kyoto if we also want nara and osaka as day trips

For a 10-day trip, a typical split is four nights in Tokyo, three in Kyoto and two in Osaka. That's nine nights, which covers the full ten days with the travel days included.

turns.user: so tokyo 4 kyoto 3 osaka 2? that's 9 nights right. feels tight but ok
turns.assistant: Yes, nine nights. It's tight but workable because the Shinkansen between Tokyo and Kyoto takes about two hours and fifteen minutes, and Kyoto to Osaka is under 20 minutes. Each move costs you half a day, so you'll want to check out in the morning and not plan anything heavy on those days. If you want more breathing room, you could drop Osaka to one night and make it a day trip from Kyoto.

turns.user: wait is nara not worth doing from osaka instead of kyoto

The Kyoto option is usually easier since you can walk from the station to Todai-ji and the deer park. If you're staying in Osaka, the Kintetsu line is an alternative, but JR is simpler for most people. Just pick whichever base you're already using so you aren't doubling back on the train.
